title: The 50/30/20 Rule — Adapted for Real Life
tagline: The textbook budget rule, and why it breaks on a ₹20,000 income in Bengaluru. How to flip it into a realistic plan that still pays you first.
summary: 50/30/20 explained, then re-engineered for a low-income, high-cost city.

sections.title: The core concept: give every rupee a job

paragraphs: A budget is not about restriction — it's about **direction**. The point is that every rupee you earn is assigned a job *before* the month starts, so money stops disappearing into a vague fog of UPI payments.
The most famous framework is the **50/30/20 rule**: split your take-home income into three buckets.

items.detail: Things you genuinely cannot skip: rent, groceries, utilities, transport to work, minimum loan payments, phone.
Lifestyle: eating out, OTT subscriptions, shopping, trips, gadgets. Life should be livable, not miserable.
Emergency fund first, then SIPs and goals. This is 'paying yourself first'.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Never let the savings bucket be the leftover. Savings is a fixed bill you pay to your future self on day one — wants flex around it, not the other way around.

paragraphs: Here's where generic advice fails. The textbook rule assumes your **needs** fit in 50% of income. For Aarav, 50% of ₹20,000 is just **₹10,000** — and in Bengaluru that doesn't cover rent and food, let alone transport. The rule isn't wrong; it's just calibrated for a higher income or cheaper city.

blocks.title: Textbook split vs Aarav's reality (₹20,000/month)
blocks.caption: On a tight income the needs bucket naturally swells. The skill is squeezing wants, not savings.

blocks.text: Aarav's real split is roughly **75/10/15**. That's fine. The 50/30/20 rule is a *target to grow into*, not a law. Every time income rises, the goal is to push the savings bucket back up toward 20%+ instead of inflating wants.

items.title: Automate the ₹3,000 on salary day
items.detail: Set a standing instruction / SIP for the 2nd of every month — the day after salary lands. If it leaves your account automatically, you can't 'forget' to save.

items.title: Use two accounts
items.detail: A 'spending' account for needs+wants, and a separate account/fund for savings. Out of sight, out of spend.

items.title: Attack the biggest lever — rent
items.detail: On a low income, rent dominates. A roommate or a PG one locality further out can free ₹2,000–3,000/month — that single change can double the savings bucket.

items.title: Track for one month, then relax
items.detail: Use any free app or a simple notes sheet for 30 days to see where money truly goes. After that, you mostly just maintain the automation.

blocks.title: Lifestyle creep is the silent killer
blocks.text: When Aarav's income rises from ₹20k to ₹30k, the instinct is to upgrade rent, food, and gadgets so wants eat the entire raise. Instead, bank at least half of every raise. A raise is the single best chance to permanently lift your savings rate.

cheatsheet: 50/30/20 = 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings — a target, not a law.
On ₹20k in Bengaluru, needs realistically take ~75%, so aim for a 75/10/15 split and grow the savings share over time.
Pay yourself first: automate savings on salary day; wants flex around it, never savings.
Rent is the biggest lever on a low income — a roommate can double your savings bucket.
Bank at least half of every future raise to beat lifestyle creep.

questions.prompt: Aarav's friend says 'the 50/30/20 rule is broken — I can't fit needs into 50% in Bengaluru, so budgeting is pointless.' What's the flaw in that reasoning?
questions.hint: Is the rule a fixed law or a target ratio?
answer: The rule is a **target to grow into**, not a hard constraint. On a tight income in a costly city, needs legitimately take more than 50% — so you run something like 75/10/15. The discipline that matters isn't hitting exactly 50/30/20; it's (a) giving every rupee a job and (b) protecting a fixed savings slice paid first.
Abandoning budgeting because the textbook ratio doesn't fit is throwing away the principle because of the label. Adapt the numbers, keep the habit.
keyPoints: Ratio is a target, not a law
Needs can exceed 50% on low income

questions.prompt: Aarav gets a raise to ₹26,000. His current savings is ₹3,000/month. What should the new savings number be, and why not just enjoy the extra ₹6,000?
questions.hint: Think about lifestyle creep and what a raise represents.
answer: He should bank at least half the raise — roughly ₹3,000 of the ₹6,000 — taking savings from ₹3,000 to about ₹6,000/month and letting the other ₹3,000 improve his lifestyle. That lifts his savings rate from 15% toward ~23%.

A raise is the best moment to permanently raise your savings rate, because you were already living on the old amount — you won't 'miss' money you never spent. If wants absorb the entire raise, his savings rate stays frozen forever even as he earns more.
keyPoints: Raises are the prime defence against lifestyle creep
You won't miss money you never started spending

questions.prompt: Why is 'save whatever is left at month-end' a near-guaranteed way to save nothing?
questions.hint: What expands to fill available money?
answer: Spending naturally expands to fill whatever money is available (Parkinson's Law for money). If savings is the leftover, there's almost never a leftover — wants quietly absorb it. Making savings the *first* automated transfer flips this: spending is now forced to fit the remainder, and the savings actually happen.
keyPoints: Automate savings first to invert the logic
